title: Chapter 5 — Necessity Of Examining The Condition Of The States Before That Of The Union At Large
paragraphs: In the following chapter I propose to examine the form of government established in America on the principle of the sovereignty of the people: what its resources are, what hinders it, what advantages it has, and what dangers. The first difficulty comes from the complex nature of the Constitution of the United States. It consists of two distinct social structures, joined together and, as it were, encased one within the other. There are two governments, completely separate and almost independent. One fulfills the ordinary duties and answers the daily and unpredictable calls of a community. The other is confined within certain limits and exercises only an exceptional authority over the general interests of the country. In short, there are twenty-four small sovereign nations, and together they make up the body of the Union. To examine the Union before we have studied the States would be to adopt a method full of obstacles. The form of the Federal Government of the United States was the last to be adopted. It is in fact nothing more than a modification or a summary of the republican principles that were already current throughout the community before it existed, and independently of its existence. Moreover, as I have just observed, the Federal Government is the exception, and the government of the States is the rule. An author who tried to present the picture as a whole before he had explained its details would inevitably fall into obscurity and repetition.

The great political principles that govern American society today undoubtedly took their origin and their growth in the State. It is therefore necessary to become acquainted with the State in order to have a clue to everything else. The States that now make up the American Union all present the same features in the outward appearance of their institutions. Their political and administrative life is centered in three focal points, which may fairly be compared to the different nerve centers that carry movement to the human body. The township is the lowest in order, then the county, and last the State. I propose to devote the following chapter to examining these three divisions.
The American System of Townships and Municipal Bodies

Why the author begins the examination of political institutions with the township—Its existence in all nations—Difficulty of establishing and preserving municipal independence—Its importance—Why the author has chosen the township system of New England as the main topic of his discussion.

It is not by accident that I begin this subject with the township. The village or township is the only association so perfectly natural that wherever a number of men are gathered together, it seems to form itself.

The town, or tithing, as the smallest division of a community, must exist in all nations, whatever their laws and customs may be. Whether men make monarchies or establish republics, the first association of mankind seems to have been formed by the hand of God. But although the township is as old as humanity, its liberties are rarely respected and are easily destroyed. A nation can always set up great political assemblies, because it ordinarily contains a certain number of individuals fitted by their talents, if not by their habits, to direct public affairs. The township, by contrast, is made of coarser material, which the legislator shapes less easily. The difficulties in the way of consolidating its independence tend to grow rather than shrink as the people become more educated. A highly civilized community scorns attempts at local independence, is disgusted by its many blunders, and is inclined to despair of success before the experiment is finished. Again, no immunities are so poorly protected against the encroachments of the supreme power as those of municipal bodies in general. They cannot struggle alone against a strong or enterprising government, and they cannot defend their cause successfully unless it is identified with the customs of the nation and supported by public opinion. Thus, until the independence of townships has fused with the mores of a people, it is easily destroyed, and it can fuse with them only after a long existence in the laws. Municipal freedom is not the fruit of human invention. It is rarely created, but it is, as it were, secretly and spontaneously born in the midst of a semi-barbarous state of society. The constant action of the laws and national habits, particular circumstances, and above all time may consolidate it. But there is certainly no nation on the continent of Europe that has experienced its advantages. Nevertheless, local assemblies of citizens are the strength of free nations. Town meetings are to liberty what primary schools are to science: they bring it within the people’s reach and teach them how to use it and enjoy it. A nation may establish a system of free government, but without the spirit of municipal institutions it cannot have the spirit of liberty. The passing passions and interests of an hour, or the chance of circumstances, may have created the outward forms of independence. But the despotic tendency that has been driven back will, sooner or later, inevitably reappear on the surface.

To explain to the reader the general principles on which the political organization of the counties and townships of the United States rests, I have thought it best to choose one of the States of New England as an example, to examine the workings of its constitution, and then to take a general look over the rest of the country. The township and the county are not organized in the same way in every part of the Union. Still, it is easy to see that the same principles guided the formation of both throughout the Union. I am inclined to believe that these principles have been carried further in New England than elsewhere, and that they therefore give a foreigner more opportunity to observe them. The institutions of New England form a complete and orderly whole. Time has sanctioned them, the laws support them, and the mores of the community support them more strongly still, and they exercise an immense influence over that community. They therefore deserve our attention on every count.
Limits of the Township

The township of New England is a division that stands between the commune and the canton of France, and it corresponds in general to the English tithing, or town. Its average population is from two to three thousand. *a So the interests of its inhabitants are unlikely to conflict, and yet men capable of conducting its affairs can always be found among its citizens.
a [ In 1830 there were 305 townships in the State of Massachusetts, and 610,014 inhabitants, which gives an average of about 2,000 inhabitants to each township.]
Authorities of the Township in New England

The people the source of all power here as elsewhere—Manages its own affairs—No corporation—The greater part of the authority vested in the hands of the Selectmen—How the Selectmen act—Town meeting—Enumeration of the public officers of the township—Obligatory and remunerated functions.

In the township, as everywhere else, the people is the only source of power. But at no other stage of government does the body of citizens exercise a more direct influence. In America the people is a master whose demands must be obeyed to the utmost limits of possibility.

In New England the majority acts through representatives in conducting the public business of the State. Such an arrangement may be necessary in general affairs, but in the townships the legislative and administrative action of the government is in closer contact with those it governs, and there the system of representation is not adopted. There is no corporation. Instead, the body of electors, after naming its magistrates, directs them in everything that goes beyond the simple, ordinary executive business of the State. *b

b [ The same rules do not apply to the great towns, which generally have a mayor and a corporation divided into two bodies. This, however, is an exception that requires the sanction of a law.—See the Act of February 22, 1822, for appointing the authorities of the city of Boston. It often happens that small towns as well as cities are subject to a special administration. In 1832, 104 townships in the State of New York were governed in this manner.—Williams’ Register.]
This state of things is so contrary to our ideas, and so different from our customs, that I must give some examples to explain it fully.

The public duties in the township are extremely numerous and minutely divided, as we shall see further on. But the larger share of administrative power is held by a small number of individuals called “the Selectmen.” *c The general laws of the State impose a certain number of obligations on the selectmen. They may fulfill these without authorization from the body they represent, but they can neglect them only at their own risk. The law of the State requires them, for instance, to draw up the list of electors in their townships, and if they omit this part of their duties, they are guilty of a misdemeanor. In all the affairs that the town meeting decides, however, the selectmen are the instruments of the popular mandate, just as in France the mayor carries out the decree of the municipal council. They usually act on their own responsibility and simply put into practice principles the majority has already recognized. But if any change is to be made in the existing state of things, or if they wish to undertake some new enterprise, they must go back to the source of their power. If, for instance, a school is to be established, the selectmen call the whole body of electors together on a certain day at an appointed place. They explain the urgency of the case. They give their opinion on the means of meeting it, on the probable expense, and on the site that seems most favorable. The meeting is consulted on each of these points. It adopts the principle, marks out the site, votes the tax, and entrusts the carrying out of its resolution to the selectmen.

c [ Three selectmen are appointed in the small townships, and nine in the large ones. See “The Town-Officer,” p. 186. See also the principal laws of the State of Massachusetts relative to the selectmen:

Act of February 20, 1786, vol. i. p. 219; February 24, 1796, vol. i. p. 488; March 7, 1801, vol. ii. p. 45; June 16, 1795, vol. i. p. 475; March 12, 1808, vol. ii. p. 186; February 28, 1787, vol. i. p. 302; June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 539.]

The selectmen alone have the right to call a town meeting, but they may be asked to do so. If ten citizens want to submit a new project to the township for its approval, they may demand a general assembly of the inhabitants. The selectmen are obliged to comply, but they have only the right to preside at the meeting. *d
d [ See Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 150, Act of March 25, 1786.]

The selectmen are elected every year in April or May. At the same time the town meeting chooses a number of other municipal magistrates, who are entrusted with important administrative functions. The assessors set the township’s tax rate, and the collectors receive the tax. A constable is appointed to keep the peace, watch the streets, and help enforce the laws. The town clerk records all the town votes, orders, grants, births, deaths, and marriages. The treasurer keeps the funds. The overseer of the poor takes on the difficult task of supervising the working of the poor laws. Committeemen are appointed to look after the schools and public instruction, and the road surveyors, who take care of the larger and smaller thoroughfares of the township, complete the list of the principal officials. These offices are, however, divided still further. Among the municipal officers are parish commissioners, who audit the expenses of public worship, and different classes of inspectors, some of whom direct the citizens in case of fire. There are also tithing-men, listers, haywards, chimney-viewers, fence-viewers to maintain property boundaries, timber-measurers, and sealers of weights and measures. *e

e [ All these magistrates actually exist; their different functions are all detailed in a book called “The Town-Officer,” by Isaac Goodwin, Worcester, 1827; and in the “Collection of the General Laws of Massachusetts,” 3 vols., Boston, 1823.]

There are nineteen principal officers in a township. Every inhabitant is required, on pain of a fine, to take on these different duties. Almost all of them are paid, however, so that poorer citizens can give up their time without loss. In general the American system does not give its officials a fixed salary. Every service has its price, and they are paid in proportion to what they have done.
Existence of the Township

Everyone the best judge of his own interest—Corollary of the principle of the sovereignty of the people—Application of these doctrines in the townships of America—The township of New England is sovereign in all that concerns itself alone, and subject to the State in all other matters—Bond between the township and the State—In France the Government lends its agent to the commune—In America the reverse occurs.

I have already observed that the principle of the sovereignty of the people governs the whole political system of the Anglo-Americans. Every page of this book will give new instances of the same doctrine. In nations that recognize the sovereignty of the people, every individual holds an equal share of power and takes an equal part in the government of the State. Every individual is therefore assumed to be as well informed, as virtuous, and as strong as any of his fellow citizens. He obeys the government, not because he is inferior to the authorities who run it, or less capable than his neighbor of governing himself, but because he acknowledges the usefulness of an association with his fellow men and knows that no such association can exist without a regulating force. In everything that concerns the mutual relations of citizens he is a subject, but in everything that concerns himself he is free and answerable to God alone. From this comes the maxim that everyone is the best and the only judge of his own private interest, and that society has no right to control a man’s actions unless they harm the common good, or unless the common good requires his cooperation. This doctrine is universally accepted in the United States. I shall examine later the general influence it has on the ordinary actions of life. For now I am speaking of the nature of municipal bodies.

The township, taken as a whole and in relation to the government of the country, may be seen as an individual to whom the theory I have just described is applied. Municipal independence is therefore a natural consequence of the principle of the sovereignty of the people in the United States. All the American republics recognize it to some degree, but circumstances have favored its growth in a particular way in New England.

In this part of the Union political activity began in the townships, and it may almost be said that each of them originally formed an independent nation. When the Kings of England asserted their supremacy, they were content to take over the central power of the State. The townships of New England remained as they had been before. Although they are now subject to the State, at first they were scarcely dependent on it. It is important to remember that they were not granted privileges. On the contrary, they gave up a portion of their independence to the State. The townships are subordinate to the State only in those interests that I shall call social, because they are common to all the citizens. In everything that concerns themselves alone they are independent. Among the inhabitants of New England I believe there is not a man who would admit that the State has any right to interfere in their local interests. The towns of New England buy and sell, sue and are sued, raise or lower their taxes, without the slightest opposition from the administrative authority of the State.

They are bound, however, to comply with the demands of the community. If the State needs money, a town can neither grant nor withhold the funds. If the State plans a road, the township cannot refuse to let it cross its territory. If the State makes a police regulation, the town must enforce it. A uniform system of instruction is organized throughout the country, and every town is obliged to establish the schools the law orders. When I speak of the administration of the United States, I shall have occasion to point out the means by which the townships are compelled to obey in these different cases. Here I merely show that the obligation exists. Strict as it is, the government of the State imposes it only in principle, and in carrying it out the township regains all its independent rights. Thus taxes are voted by the State, but they are levied and collected by the township. The existence of a school is compulsory, but the township builds it, pays for it, and supervises it. In France the State’s tax collector receives the local taxes. In America the town’s collector receives the taxes of the State. Thus the French government lends its agents to the commune, whereas in America the township is the agent of the government. This fact alone shows how great the differences are between the two nations.
Public Spirit of the Townships of New England

How the township of New England wins the affections of its inhabitants—Difficulty of creating local public spirit in Europe—The rights and duties of the American township favorable to it—Characteristics of home in the United States—Manifestations of public spirit in New England—Its happy effects.

In America municipal bodies not only exist, but public spirit keeps them alive and supports them. The township of New England has two advantages that unfailingly secure the attentive interest of mankind, namely independence and authority. Its sphere is indeed small and limited, but within that sphere its action is unrestrained. Its independence gives it a real importance that its size and population might not always ensure.

We should remember that men’s affections generally lie on the side of authority. Patriotism does not last in a conquered nation. The New Englander is attached to his township not only because he was born in it, but because it is a social body of which he is a member, and because its government claims, and deserves, the use of his judgment. In Europe, those in power often regret the absence of local public spirit. Everyone agrees that there is no surer guarantee of order and tranquility, and yet nothing is harder to create. If municipal bodies were made powerful and independent, the authorities of the nation might be divided and the peace of the country endangered. Yet without power and independence, a town may contain good subjects, but it can have no active citizens. Another important fact is that the township of New England is so constituted as to arouse the warmest of human affections without awakening the ambitious passions of the human heart. The officers of the county are not elected, and their authority is very limited. Even the State is only a second-rate community, whose quiet and obscure administration offers no inducement strong enough to draw men away from the circle of their own interests into the turmoil of public affairs. The federal government confers power and honor on the men who run it, but those individuals can never be very numerous. The high office of the Presidency can be reached only late in life, and the other federal officials are generally men who have been favored by fortune or have distinguished themselves in some other career. Such offices cannot be the permanent aim of the ambitious. But the township serves as a center for the desire of public esteem, the need for stimulating interests, and the taste for authority and popularity, all within the ordinary relations of life. The passions that commonly embroil society change their character when they find an outlet so near the domestic hearth and the family circle.

In the American States power has been distributed with admirable skill in order to interest the greatest possible number of persons in the common good. Apart from the electors, who are called into action from time to time, the body politic is divided among innumerable officials and officers. Each, in his own sphere, represents the same powerful whole in whose name he acts. Local administration thus provides an unfailing source of profit and interest to a vast number of individuals.

The American system divides local authority among so many citizens, and it does not hesitate to multiply the functions of the town officers. For in the United States it is believed, and with truth, that patriotism is a kind of devotion that is strengthened by ritual observance. In this way the activity of the township is continually felt. It shows itself daily in the fulfillment of a duty or the exercise of a right, and a constant but gentle motion is thus kept up in society, which stirs it without disturbing it.

The American attaches himself to his home as the mountaineer clings to his hills, because the distinctive features of his country are marked more clearly there than elsewhere. The townships of New England are in general happy. Their government suits their tastes and is chosen by themselves. In the midst of the profound peace and general comfort that reign in America, the upheavals of municipal discord are rare. The conduct of local business is easy. The political education of the people has long been complete. Or rather, it was complete when the people first set foot on the soil. In New England there is no tradition of a distinction of ranks. No part of the community is tempted to oppress the rest, and the abuses that may injure isolated individuals are forgotten in the general contentment that prevails. The government may be defective (and no doubt it would be easy to point out its defects). Still, the fact that it really comes from those it governs, and that it acts, whether badly or well, casts over its faults the protective spell of a parent’s pride. No point of comparison disturbs the citizen’s satisfaction. England once governed the mass of the colonies, but the people was always sovereign in the township, where its rule is not only an ancient state of things but a primitive one.

The native of New England is attached to his township because it is independent and free. His share in its affairs ensures his attachment to its interest. The well-being it gives him secures his affection, and its welfare is the aim of his ambition and of his future efforts. He takes part in every event in the place. He practices the art of government in the small sphere within his reach. He accustoms himself to those forms that alone can ensure the steady progress of liberty, and he absorbs their spirit. He acquires a taste for order, understands the union or the balance of powers, and gathers clear, practical ideas about the nature of his duties and the extent of his rights.
The Counties of New England

The division of the counties in America is very similar to that of the arrondissements of France. The boundaries of the counties are laid down arbitrarily, and the various districts they contain have no necessary connection, no common tradition and no natural sympathy. Their purpose is simply to make the administration of justice easier.

The township was too small to contain a system of judicial institutions. Each county, however, has a court of justice, *f a sheriff to carry out its decrees, and a prison for criminals. There are certain needs that all the townships of a county feel alike, so it is natural that a central authority should meet them. In the State of Massachusetts this authority is held by several magistrates, who are appointed by the Governor of the State with the advice *g of his council. *h The officers of the county have only a limited and occasional authority, which applies to certain predetermined cases. The State and the townships hold all the power needed to conduct public business. The county’s budget is drawn up by its officers and voted by the legislature, but no assembly directly or indirectly represents the county. Properly speaking, therefore, it has no political existence.
f [ See the Act of February 14, 1821, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 551.]
g [ See the Act of February 20, 1819, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. ii. p. 494.]

h [ The council of the Governor is an elective body.] A twofold tendency can be seen in the American constitutions. It drives the legislator to centralize legislative power and to disperse executive power. The township of New England has within itself an indestructible element of independence, and this separate existence could be introduced into the county only artificially, since there its usefulness has not been felt. But all the townships together have only one representation, which is the State, the center of the national authority. Beyond the action of the township and that of the nation, nothing can be said to exist except the influence of individual effort.
Administration in New England

Administration not perceived in America—Why?—Europeans believe that liberty is promoted by depriving the social authority of some of its rights; Americans, by dividing its exercise—Almost all administration confined to the township and divided among the town officers—No trace of an administrative body to be perceived, either in the township or above it—The reason for this—How it happens that the administration of the State is uniform—Who is empowered to enforce the obedience of the township and the county to the law—The introduction of judicial power into the administration—Consequence of extending the elective principle to all officials—The Justice of the Peace in New England—By whom appointed—County officer: ensures the administration of the townships—Court of Sessions—Its action—Right of inspection and indictment distributed like the other administrative functions—Informers encouraged by the division of fines.

Nothing strikes a European traveler in the United States more than the absence of what we call the government, or the administration. Written laws exist in America, and one sees them carried out every day. But although everything is in motion, the hand that sets the social machine going cannot be found anywhere. Nevertheless, all peoples must use certain grammatical forms, which are the foundation of human language, in order to express their thoughts. In the same way, all communities must secure their existence by submitting to a certain amount of authority, without which they fall prey to anarchy. This authority may be distributed in several ways, but it must always exist somewhere.

There are two ways of reducing the force of authority in a nation. The first is to weaken the supreme power at its very root, by forbidding or preventing society from acting in its own defense under certain circumstances. To weaken authority in this way is what is generally called in Europe laying the foundations of freedom. The second way of reducing the influence of authority does not strip society of any of its rights or paralyze its efforts. Instead, it distributes the exercise of its privileges among various hands and multiplies the officials, each of whom is entrusted with the degree of power he needs to do his duty. There may be nations for whom this distribution of social powers might lead to anarchy. But in itself it is not anarchical. The action of authority is indeed made less irresistible and less perilous in this way, but it is not suppressed altogether.

The revolution of the United States was the result of a mature and dignified taste for freedom, not of a vague and ill-defined craving for independence. It made no alliance with the turbulent passions of anarchy. On the contrary, its course was marked by an attachment to whatever was lawful and orderly.

It was never assumed in the United States that the citizen of a free country has the right to do whatever he pleases. On the contrary, more varied social obligations were imposed on him there than anywhere else. No one ever thought of attacking the principles of society or contesting its rights. But the exercise of its authority was divided, so that the office might be powerful and the officeholder insignificant, and so that the community might be at once regulated and free. In no country in the world does the law speak so absolute a language as in America, and in no country is the right to apply it placed in so many hands. The administrative power in the United States is neither central nor hierarchical in its makeup, and this is why it passes unnoticed. The power exists, but its representative cannot be seen.

We have already seen that the independent townships of New England look after their own private interests. The municipal magistrates are the people most often entrusted with carrying out the laws of the State. *i Besides the general laws, the State sometimes passes general police regulations. More commonly, though, the townships and town officers, together with justices of the peace, regulate the minor details of social life according to the needs of the different localities. They issue such rules as concern the health of the community and the peace and morality of the citizens. *j Finally, these municipal magistrates provide, on their own initiative and without any delegated powers, for the unforeseen emergencies that often arise in society. *k

i [ See “The Town-Officer,” especially at the words Selectmen, Assessors, Collectors, Schools, Surveyors of Highways. I take one example in a thousand: the State prohibits traveling on Sunday; the tything-men, who are town officers, are specially charged with keeping watch and enforcing the law. See the Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 410.
The selectmen draw up the lists of electors for the election of the Governor, and send the result of the ballot to the Secretary of the State. See Act of February 24, 1796: Id., vol. i. p. 488.]

j [ Thus, for instance, the selectmen authorize the construction of drains and point out the proper sites for slaughterhouses and other trades that are a nuisance to the neighborhood. See the Act of June 7, 1785: Id., vol. i. p. 193.]
k [ The selectmen take measures for the security of the public in case of contagious diseases, together with the justices of the peace. See Act of June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 539.]

It follows from what we have said that in the State of Massachusetts the administrative authority is almost entirely restricted to the township, *l but that it is distributed among a great number of individuals. In the French commune there is properly only one official, the mayor. In New England, as we have seen, there are nineteen. These nineteen officials do not in general depend on one another. The law carefully marks out a sphere of action for each of these magistrates, and within that sphere each has a full right to carry out his duties independently of any other authority. Above the township scarcely any trace of a ranked series of officials is to be found. It sometimes happens that the county officers alter a decision of the townships or town magistrates. *m But in general the authorities of the county have no right to interfere with the authorities of the township, *n except in matters that concern the county.

l [ I say almost, because some matters in the life of a township are regulated by a justice of the peace acting alone, or by the justices of the peace assembled in the chief town of the county. Licenses, for example, are granted by the justices. See the Act of February 28, 1787, vol. i. p. 297.]

m [ Thus licenses are granted only to those who can produce a certificate of good conduct from the selectmen. If the selectmen refuse to give the certificate, the applicant may appeal to the justices assembled in the Court of Sessions, who may then grant the license. See Act of March 12, 1808, vol. ii. p. 186.
The townships have the right to make by-laws and to enforce them with fines set by law, but the Court of Sessions must approve these by-laws. See Act of March 23, 1786, vol. i. p. 254.]

n [ In Massachusetts the county magistrates are often called on to investigate the acts of the town magistrates. But it will be shown further on that this investigation results from their judicial power, not their administrative power.]

The magistrates of the township, like those of the county, are bound to report their acts to the central government in a very small number of predetermined cases. *o But the central government is not represented by any individual whose business it is to publish police regulations and ordinances enforcing the execution of the laws, to keep up regular communication with the officers of the township and the county, to inspect their conduct, to direct their actions, or to reprimand their faults. There is no point that serves as a center for the radii of the administration.
o [ The town committees of schools are obliged to make an annual report to the Secretary of the State on the condition of the school. See Act of March 10, 1827, vol. iii. p. 183.]

What, then, is the uniform plan on which the government is conducted, and how is compliance enforced on the counties and their magistrates, or on the townships and their officers? In the States of New England the legislative authority covers more subjects than it does in France. The legislator reaches to the very core of the administration. The law goes down to the smallest details. The same enactment lays down both the principle and the method of applying it, and so imposes a multitude of strict and rigorously defined obligations on the secondary officials of the State. The consequence is that if all the secondary officials of the administration conform to the law, society in all its branches moves with the greatest uniformity. The difficulty that remains is how to compel the secondary officials of the administration to conform to the law. It may be affirmed that, in general, society has only two methods at its disposal for enforcing the execution of the laws. One is to give a superior official discretionary power to direct all the others and to dismiss them if they disobey. The other is to authorize the courts of justice to inflict judicial penalties on the offender. But these two methods are not always available.

The right to direct a civil officer presupposes the right to dismiss him if he does not obey orders, and to reward him by promotion if he does his duty properly. But an elected magistrate can be neither dismissed nor promoted. All elective offices are inalienable until their term has expired. In fact, the elected magistrate has nothing to expect or to fear from his constituents. And when all public offices are filled by ballot, there can be no ranked series of official dignities. The double right of commanding and of enforcing obedience can never be vested in the same individual, and the power to give an order can never be joined to the power to inflict a punishment or give a reward.

Communities in which the secondary officials of the government are elected are therefore forced to make great use of judicial penalties as a means of administration. This is not obvious at first sight. Those in power tend to regard the institution of elective officials as one concession, and the subjection of the elected magistrate to the judges of the land as another. They dislike both these innovations equally. And since they are pressed more urgently to grant the first than the second, they agree to the election of the magistrate and leave him independent of the judicial power. Nevertheless, the second measure is the only thing that can possibly counterbalance the first. It will be found that an elective authority that is not subject to judicial power will, sooner or later, either escape all control or be destroyed. The courts of justice are the only possible intermediary between the central power and the administrative bodies. They alone can compel the elected official to obey without violating the rights of the elector. The extension of judicial power in the political world ought therefore to be in exact proportion to the extension of elective offices. If these two institutions do not go hand in hand, the state must fall into anarchy or into subjection.

People have always noticed that the habits of legal business do not prepare men to exercise administrative authority. The Americans took from the English, their forefathers, an institution that the continent of Europe does not know: the Justices of the Peace. The Justice of the Peace stands halfway between the magistrate and the ordinary man of the world, between the civil officer and the judge. He is a well-informed citizen, though not necessarily someone trained in the law. His office simply requires him to enforce the police regulations of society, and for that task good sense and integrity count for more than legal science. The justice brings to the administration a certain taste for established forms and for publicity, which makes him a most unserviceable instrument of despotism. At the same time, he is free of the superstitions that make legal officers poor members of a government. The Americans have adopted the English system of justices of the peace, but they have removed the aristocratic character it has in the mother country. The Governor of Massachusetts *p appoints a certain number of justices of the peace in every county, for terms of seven years. *q He also chooses three of them from the whole body of justices, and in each county these three form what is called the Court of Sessions. The justices take a personal share in public business. Sometimes they receive administrative functions alongside elected officers, *r and sometimes they form a tribunal before which the magistrates summarily prosecute a refractory citizen, or the citizens report abuses by a magistrate. But the Court of Sessions is where they exercise their most important functions. This court meets twice a year in the county town, and in Massachusetts it has the power to enforce the obedience of most *s public officers. *t It should be noted that in Massachusetts the Court of Sessions is at once an administrative body in the proper sense and a political tribunal. Some have claimed that the county is a purely administrative division. The Court of Sessions handles the few affairs that concern several townships, or all the townships of the county in common, and that therefore cannot be left to any one of them. *u In everything that concerns county business, its duties are purely administrative. If in its investigations it sometimes borrows the forms of judicial procedure, it does so only to inform itself, *v or as a guarantee to the community it presides over. But when the administration of a township is brought before it, it always acts as a judicial body, and in a few cases as an official assembly.
p [ We shall learn later what a Governor is. I will content myself here with noting that he represents the executive power of the whole State.]
q [ See the Constitution of Massachusetts, chap. II. sect. 1. Section 9; chap. III. Section 3.]

r [ Thus, for example, a stranger arrives in a township from a country where a contagious disease prevails, and he falls ill. Two justices of the peace can, with the assent of the selectmen, order the sheriff of the county to remove him and look after him.—Act of June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 540.

In general the justices take part in all the important acts of the administration and give them a semi-judicial character.] [Footnote s: I say most, because certain administrative misdemeanors are brought before ordinary tribunals. If, for instance, a township refuses to make the necessary expenditure for its schools or to name a school committee, it is liable to a heavy fine. But this penalty is pronounced by the Supreme Judicial Court or the Court of Common Pleas. See Act of March 10, 1827, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. iii. p. 190. The same is true when a township neglects to provide the necessary war supplies.—Act of February 21, 1822: Id., vol. ii. p. 570.]

t [ In their individual capacity the justices of the peace take part in the business of the counties and townships.] [Footnote u: These affairs can be grouped under the following heads:—1. The building of prisons and courthouses. 2. The county budget, which is afterward voted by the State. 3. The distribution of the taxes so voted. 4. The granting of certain patents. 5. The laying out and repair of the county roads.]
v [ Thus, when a road is under consideration, almost all difficulties are settled with the help of the jury.]

The first difficulty is getting obedience from an authority as entirely independent of the State’s general laws as the township is. We have said that the town meetings name assessors every year to levy the taxes. Suppose a township tries to avoid paying taxes by failing to name its assessors. The Court of Sessions then sentences it to a heavy penalty. *w The fine falls on each of the inhabitants, and the sheriff of the county, who is the officer of justice, carries out the order. In this way, in the United States, the authority of the government hides mysteriously behind the forms of a judicial sentence, and at the same time it gains strength from the irresistible power that people have given to the formalities of law.
w [ See Act of February 20, 1786, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 217.]

These proceedings are easy to follow and to understand. The demands made on a township are in general plain and exactly defined; they consist of a simple fact without any complication, or of a principle without detailed application. *x But the difficulty grows when what must be enforced is not the obedience of the township but that of the town officers. All the blameworthy actions of which a public official may be guilty can be reduced to the following heads:

x [ There is an indirect method of enforcing the obedience of a township. Suppose that the funds the law requires for the upkeep of the roads have not been voted. The town surveyor is then authorized, ex officio, to raise the money. Since he is personally liable to private individuals for the state of the roads, and can be indicted before the Court of Sessions, he is sure to use the extraordinary right the law gives him against the township. Thus, by threatening the officer, the Court of Sessions extracts compliance from the town. See Act of March 5, 1787, Id., vol. i. p. 305.]
He may carry out the law without energy or zeal;
He may neglect to carry out the law;
He may do what the law forbids him to do.

Only the last two violations of duty can come before a tribunal, because an action at law needs a positive, measurable fact as its foundation. Thus the selectmen may be fined if they fail to follow the legal formalities customary at town elections; *y but when a public officer does his duty badly, or obeys the letter of the law without zeal or energy, he is at least safe from judicial interference. Here even the Court of Sessions, with its full official powers, cannot force him into more satisfactory obedience. Fear of removal is the only check on such quasi-offences, and since the Court of Sessions does not create the town authorities, it cannot remove officials it does not appoint. Besides, proving negligence or lukewarmness would take constant investigation, while the Court of Sessions sits only twice a year and judges only the offences that are brought to its attention. A court of justice cannot impose that active and enlightened obedience on public officers; the only security for it is the possibility of removing them at will. In France this security is sought in the powers of the heads of the administration; in America it is sought in the principle of election.
y [ Laws of Massachusetts, vol. ii. p. 45.]

To sum up in a few words what I have been showing: if a public officer in New England commits a crime in the exercise of his functions, the ordinary courts of justice are always called on to sentence him. If he commits a fault in his official capacity, a purely administrative tribunal has the power to punish him; and if the matter is important or urgent, the judge makes up for what the officer failed to do. *z Finally, if the same man is guilty of one of those intangible offences that human justice does not notice, he must appear every year before a tribunal from which there is no appeal, one that can at once reduce him to insignificance and take away his office. This system undoubtedly has great advantages, but putting it into practice involves a difficulty that deserves to be pointed out.

z [ If, for instance, a township persists in refusing to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions appoints them, and the magistrates so appointed have the same authority as elected officers. See the Act quoted above, February 20, 1787.]

I have already observed that the administrative tribunal called the Court of Sessions has no right to inspect the town officers. It can step in only when the conduct of a magistrate is specifically brought to its attention, and this is the delicate part of the system. The Americans of New England have no public prosecutor in the Court of Sessions, *a and it is easy to see that creating one would have been difficult. Suppose an accusing magistrate had been appointed only in the chief town of each county, with no agents to help him in the townships. He would have known no more about what was going on in the county than the members of the Court of Sessions. But appointing agents in every township would have placed in his hands the most formidable of powers, that of a judicial administration. Besides, laws are the children of habit, and nothing of the kind exists in English legislation. The Americans have therefore divided the functions of inspection and prosecution, as they have divided all the other functions of the administration. The law requires grand jurors to inform the court to which they belong of every misdemeanor committed in their county. *b Certain great offences are prosecuted officially by the States; *c but more often the job of punishing offenders falls to the fiscal officer, whose duty it is to receive the fine. Thus the treasurer of the township is responsible for prosecuting the administrative offences that come to his notice. But American legislation also appeals in a more particular way to the private interest of the citizen; *d and anyone studying the laws of the United States meets this great principle constantly. American legislators are readier to credit men with intelligence than with honesty, and they count heavily on personal greed to get the laws carried out. When someone is really and noticeably harmed by an administrative abuse, it is natural that his own interest should lead him to prosecute. But suppose a legal formality is required that benefits the community yet matters little to individuals. Plaintiffs may then be harder to find, and by a tacit agreement the laws may fall into disuse. Their system has brought the Americans to this extreme, and so they are obliged to encourage informers by giving them a share of the penalty in certain cases, *e and to secure the execution of the laws by the dangerous expedient of degrading the morals of the people. The only administrative authority above the county magistrates is, properly speaking, that of the government.
a [ I say the Court of Sessions, because in common courts there is a magistrate who exercises some of the functions of a public prosecutor.]
b [ The grand-jurors are, for instance, bound to inform the court of the bad state of the roads.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 308.]

c [ If, for instance, the treasurer of the county holds back his accounts.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 406.] [Footnote d: Thus, if a private individual suffers a breakdown or is injured because of the bad state of a road, he can sue the township or the county for damages at the sessions.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 309.]

e [ In cases of invasion or insurrection, if the town officers neglect to furnish the necessary stores and ammunition for the militia, the township may be sentenced to a fine of from $200 to $500. One can easily imagine that in such a case no one might care to prosecute; hence the law adds that any citizen may bring an indictment for offences of this kind, and that half of the fine shall go to the plaintiff. See Act of March 6, 1810, vol. ii. p. 236. The same clause is frequently found in the law of Massachusetts. Private individuals are not only encouraged in this way to prosecute public officers; public officers are likewise encouraged to bring the disobedience of private individuals to justice. If a citizen refuses to do the work assigned to him on a road, the road surveyor may prosecute him, and he receives half the penalty for himself. See the Laws cited above, vol. i. p. 308.]

General Remarks on the Administration of the United States Differences among the States of the Union in their systems of administration—Activity and perfection of the local authorities decrease toward the South—Power of the magistrate increases; that of the elector diminishes—Administration passes from the township to the county—States of New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania—Principles of administration applicable to the whole Union—Election of public officers, and inalienability of their functions—Absence of gradation of ranks—Introduction of judicial resources into the administration.

I said earlier that, after examining the constitution of the township and the county in New England in detail, I would take a general view of the rest of the Union. Every State has townships and local activity, but nowhere in the confederation will we find a township exactly like those of New England. The farther south we go, the less active the business of the township or parish becomes. There are fewer magistrates, functions, and rights; the population has a less direct influence on affairs; town meetings are less frequent and have fewer subjects to debate. The elected magistrate gains power and the elector loses it, while the public spirit of local communities is less awake and less influential. *f We can see these differences to some extent in New York; they are very noticeable in Pennsylvania; and they grow less striking as we move toward the northwest. Most emigrants who settle in the northwestern States are natives of New England, and they bring the habits of their mother country into the one they adopt. A township in Ohio is by no means unlike a township in Massachusetts.
f [ For details see the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. pp. 336-364, entitled, “Of the Powers, Duties, and Privileges of Towns.”

See in the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, the words Assessors, Collector, Constables, Overseer of the Poor, Supervisors of Highways; and in the Acts of a general nature of the State of Ohio, the Act of February 25, 1834, relating to townships, p. 412; besides the particular provisions relating to various town officers, such as Township’s Clerk, Trustees, Overseers of the Poor, Fence Viewers, Appraisers of Property, Township’s Treasurer, Constables, Supervisors of Highways.]

We have seen that in Massachusetts the mainspring of public administration is the township, which is the common center of the citizens’ interests and affections. This stops being true as we go down to States where knowledge is less widely spread and where the township therefore offers fewer guarantees of a wise and active administration. As we leave New England, we find the importance of the town passing gradually to the county. The county becomes the center of administration and the intermediate power between the government and the citizen. In Massachusetts a Court of Sessions conducts county business, and it is made up of a quorum named by the Governor and his council; the county has no representative assembly, and the national legislature votes its expenditure. In the great State of New York, by contrast, and in Ohio and Pennsylvania, the inhabitants of each county choose a number of representatives, who form the county assembly. *g This assembly may tax the inhabitants to a certain extent, and in this respect it has the privileges of a real legislative body. It also exercises executive power in the county, often directs the administration of the townships, and keeps their authority within much narrower limits than in Massachusetts.

g [ See the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. p. 340. Id. chap. xii. p. 366; also in the Acts of the State of Ohio, an act relating to county commissioners, February 25, 1824, p. 263. See the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, at the words County-rates and Levies, p. 170. In the State of New York each township elects a representative, who takes part in the administration of the county as well as in that of the township.]

Those are the main differences between the systems of county and town administration in the Federal States. If I meant to examine American law in minute detail, I would have to point out still more differences in how the several communities carry out their business. But what I have said is enough to show the general principles on which administration in the United States rests. These principles are applied in different ways, and they produce more or fewer consequences from place to place, but they remain substantially the same. The laws differ and their outward features change; their character does not. The township and the county are not set up the same way everywhere, yet in the United States both always rest on one principle: each person is the best judge of what concerns himself alone, and the best person to meet his own private needs. So the township and the county must look after their own special interests. The State governs, but it does not interfere in how they administer them. We may find exceptions to this rule, but never a contrary principle.

The first consequence of this doctrine is that all the magistrates are chosen either by the citizens or at least from among them. Officers are everywhere elected or appointed for a fixed term, so it was impossible to set up a dependent chain of authorities. There are almost as many independent officials as there are functions, and the executive power is scattered among a multitude of hands. This made it indispensable to bring the administration under the control of the courts of justice, and to use a system of pecuniary penalties to force the secondary bodies and their representatives to obey the laws. This system prevails from one end of the Union to the other. The States have not, however, all given the same judges the power to punish misconduct by public officers, or to act as the executive in urgent cases. The Anglo-Americans took the institution of justices of the peace from a common source, but although it exists in all the States, it is not always put to the same use. Everywhere the justices of the peace take part in administering the townships and the counties, *h either as public officers or as judges of public misdemeanors; but in most of the States the more important classes of public offences go before the ordinary tribunals.
h [ In some of the Southern States the county courts are charged with all the details of the administration. See the Statutes of the State of Tennessee, arts. Judiciary, Taxes, etc.]

Election of public officers, or the inalienability of their functions; the absence of any gradation of powers; judicial control over the secondary branches of the administration: these are the features found everywhere in the American system, from Maine to the Floridas. In some States traces of a centralized administration begin to show, and New York has gone furthest in this direction. In New York the officers of the central government sometimes exercise a kind of inspection or control over the secondary bodies. *i

i [ For instance, the direction of public instruction is centered in the hands of the government. The legislature names the members of the University, who are called Regents; the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor of the State are necessarily among them.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455. The Regents of the University visit the colleges and academies every year and report to the legislature. Their supervision is not ineffective, for several reasons: colleges, in order to become corporations, need a charter, which is granted only on the recommendation of the Regents; every year funds are distributed by the State to encourage learning, and the Regents distribute this money. See chap. xv. “Instruction,” Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455.
The school commissioners are required to send an annual report to the Superintendent of the Republic.—Id. p. 488.
A similar report is made every year to the same person on the number and condition of the poor.—Id. p. 631.]

At other times they form a court of appeal for deciding affairs. *j In New York, judicial penalties are used less than elsewhere as a means of administration, and the right to prosecute offences by public officers is placed in fewer hands. *k The same tendency can faintly be seen in some other States; *l but in general the most prominent feature of administration in the United States is its excessive local independence.

j [ If anyone believes himself wronged by the school commissioners (who are town officers), he can appeal to the superintendent of the primary schools, whose decision is final.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 487.

Provisions similar to those cited above are found from time to time in the laws of the State of New York; but in general these attempts at centralization are weak and unproductive. The great authorities of the State have the right to watch and control the subordinate agents, but not to reward or punish them. The same individual is never empowered both to give an order and to punish disobedience; he therefore has the right to command without the means of exacting compliance. In 1830 the Superintendent of Schools complained in his Annual Report to the legislature that several school commissioners had neglected, despite his request, to send him the accounts that were due. He added that if this omission continued, he would be obliged to prosecute them, as the law directs, before the proper tribunals.]
k [ Thus the district attorney is directed to recover all fines below the sum of fifty dollars, unless that right has been specially given to another magistrate.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 383.]

l [ Several traces of centralization can be found in Massachusetts; for instance, the committees of the town schools are directed to make an annual report to the Secretary of State. See Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 367.]

I have described the townships and the administration. It now remains for me to speak of the State and its government. I can cover this ground quickly without fear of being misunderstood, for all I have to say is found in the written forms of the various constitutions, which are easy to obtain. These constitutions rest on a simple and rational theory. All constitutional nations have adopted their forms, and we know them well. So I need give only a short analysis here, and I shall try afterward to pass judgment on what I now describe.
Legislative Power of the State
Division of the Legislative Body into Two Houses—Senate—House of Representatives—Different Functions of These Two Bodies.

The legislative power of the State rests in two assemblies; the first usually carries the name of Senate. The Senate is normally a legislative body, but at times it also acts as an executive and judicial one. How it takes part in government varies with the constitutions of the different States; *m but it most often exercises executive power in nominating public officers. It shares in judicial power when certain political offences are tried, and sometimes when certain civil cases are decided. *n It always has few members. The other branch of the legislature, usually called the House of Representatives, has no share at all in the administration. It takes part in judicial power only by impeaching public officers before the Senate. Almost everywhere the members of the two Houses are subject to the same conditions of election, and are chosen in the same way by the same citizens. The one difference between them is that senators are generally chosen for a longer term than representatives. Representatives seldom stay in office more than a year; senators usually sit two or three years. Because senators may be chosen for several years and are renewed in rotation, the law keeps in the legislative body a nucleus of men who are already used to public business and who can have a salutary influence on the junior members.
m [ In Massachusetts the Senate is not invested with any administrative functions.]
n [ As in the State of New York.]

The Americans clearly did not mean, by dividing the legislative body into two branches, to make one house hereditary and the other elected, one aristocratic and the other democratic. Their purpose was not to make the one a bulwark of power while the other represented the interests and passions of the people. The present constitution of the United States gives only these advantages: the legislative power is divided, which checks political assemblies, and there is a tribunal of appeal for revising the laws.

Time and experience, however, have convinced the Americans that, even if these are its only advantages, dividing the legislative power is still a principle of the greatest necessity. Pennsylvania was the only one of the United States that at first tried to set up a single House of Assembly. Franklin himself was so swept along by the necessary consequences of the principle of the sovereignty of the people that he went along with it. But the Pennsylvanians soon had to change the law and create two Houses. So the principle of dividing the legislative power was finally established, and its necessity can now be regarded as a demonstrated truth. The republics of antiquity hardly knew this theory. It entered the world almost by accident, as so many other great truths have, and several modern nations have misunderstood it. At last it has become an axiom of the political science of our age.
[See Benjamin Franklin]
The Executive Power of the State
Office of Governor in an American State—The place he occupies in relation to the legislature—His rights and his duties—His dependence on the people.

It may truly be said that the Governor represents the executive power of the State, although he holds only a portion of its rights. The supreme magistrate, with the title of Governor, is the official moderator and counselor of the legislature. He has a veto, or suspensive power, with which he can stop its movements or at least delay them as he pleases. He lays the needs of the country before the legislative body and points out the means he thinks could usefully be used to meet them. In every undertaking that concerns the nation at large, he is the natural executor of the legislature’s decrees. *o When the legislature is not in session, the Governor must take every necessary step to protect the State from violent shocks and unforeseen dangers. The whole military power of the State is at his disposal. He commands the militia and heads the armed force. When the authority that people generally agree to give the laws is disregarded, the Governor puts himself at the head of the State’s armed force to put down resistance and restore order. Lastly, the Governor has no share in administering townships and counties, except indirectly through nominating Justices of the Peace, a nomination he cannot cancel. *p The Governor is an elected magistrate, usually chosen for only one or two years, so he always remains strictly dependent on the majority that elected him.

o [ In practice, it is not always the Governor who carries out the plans of the legislature; it often happens that the legislature, in voting a measure, names special agents to oversee its execution.]
p [ In some of the States the justices of the peace are not chosen by the Governor.]
Political Effects of the System of Local Administration in the United States

Necessary distinction between the general centralization of government and the centralization of the local administration—Local administration not centralized in the United States: great general centralization of the government—Some bad consequences resulting to the United States from the local administration—Administrative advantages of this order of things—The power that conducts the government is less regular, less enlightened, less learned, but much greater than in Europe—Political advantages of this order of things—In the United States the interests of the country are everywhere kept in view—Support given to the government by the community—Provincial institutions more necessary as the social condition becomes more democratic—Reason for this.

Centralization has become a word in general, daily use, though no precise meaning is attached to it. Yet there are two distinct kinds of centralization, and we must carefully tell them apart. Some interests are common to all parts of a nation, such as enacting its general laws and conducting its foreign relations. Other interests belong to particular parts of the nation, such as the business of the different townships. When the power that directs the general interests is gathered in one place, or held by the same persons, it forms a central government. In the same way, when the power of directing partial or local interests is brought together in one place, it forms what may be called a central administration.

On some points the two kinds of centralization merge, but if we sort the matters that fall more particularly within the province of each, we can easily tell them apart. Clearly, a central government gains immense power when it is joined to administrative centralization. In that combination it teaches men to set their own will aside habitually and completely, to submit not just once or on one point but in every respect and at all times. So this union of power does more than subdue them by force. It also affects them in the ordinary habits of life, and it influences each individual, first separately and then collectively.

These two kinds of centralization help and draw each other on, but we should not think them inseparable. One cannot imagine a more completely central government than the one France had under Louis XIV. The same man made the laws and interpreted them, and he represented France at home and abroad, so he was justified in claiming that the State was identified with his person. Even so, the administration was much less centralized under Louis XIV than it is today.

In England the centralization of the government is carried to great perfection. The State has the compact vigor of a single man; by an act of its will alone it sets immense machinery in motion and wields or gathers the efforts of its authority. Indeed, I cannot conceive that a nation can have a secure or prosperous existence without a powerful centralization of government. But I think that a central administration saps the strength of the nations in which it exists, because it constantly weakens their public spirit. Such an administration may succeed, at a given moment and at a given point, in gathering all the available resources of a people. Even so, it at least harms the renewal of those resources. It may secure victory in the hour of struggle, but it slowly loosens the sinews of strength. It can do wonders for the passing greatness of one man; it cannot ensure the lasting prosperity of a nation.

If we look carefully, we shall find that whenever people say a State cannot act because it has no central point, what it lacks is centralization of government. People often claim, and we are ready to believe, that the German empire never managed to bring all its powers into action. The reason was that the State could never enforce obedience to its general laws. The several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, to refuse their cooperation to the representatives of the common authority, even in matters that concerned the mass of the people. In other words, there was no centralization of government. The same remark applies to the Middle Ages. All the confusion of feudal society came from this: control over general interests, as well as local ones, was divided among a thousand hands and broken up in a thousand ways. Without a central government, the nations of Europe could not move energetically along any straight course.

We have shown that the United States has no central administration and no dependent chain of public officials. Local authority has been pushed to lengths that no European nation could tolerate without great inconvenience, and that have even had some harmful results in America. But in the United States the centralization of the government is complete, and it would be easy to prove that the national power is more compact than it has ever been in the old nations of Europe. Each State has only one legislative body and only one source of political authority. District assemblies and county courts have generally not been multiplied, for fear that they might be tempted to go beyond their administrative duties and interfere with the government. In America the legislature of each State is supreme. Nothing can impede its authority: not privileges, not local immunities, not personal influence, not even the empire of reason, since the legislature represents the majority, which claims to be the sole organ of reason. Its own decision is therefore the only limit on its action. Beside it, and under its immediate control, stands the representative of the executive power, whose duty is to make the refractory submit by superior force. The only sign of weakness lies in certain details of how the government acts. The American republics have no standing armies to intimidate a discontented minority; but no minority has yet been driven to declare open war, so the need for an army has not been felt. *q The State usually uses the officers of the township or the county to deal with the citizens. Thus, in New England, the assessor sets the rate of taxes, the collector receives them, the town treasurer sends the amount to the public treasury, and any disputes that arise go before the ordinary courts of justice. This way of collecting taxes is slow as well as inconvenient, and it would be a permanent hindrance to a government with large financial demands. In whatever materially affects its existence, the government ought to be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at will, and used to rapid methods of proceeding. But it will always be easy for the central government, organized as it is in America, to introduce new and more effective ways of acting, suited to its needs. [Footnote q: [The Civil War of 1860-65 cruelly belied this statement, and in the course of the struggle the North alone called two and a half million men to arms; but to the honor of the United States it must be added that, when the contest ended, this army disappeared as rapidly as it had been raised.—Translator’s Note.]]

The absence of a central government will not, then, prove the destruction of the republics of the New World, as has often been claimed. Far from supposing that the American governments are not centralized enough, I shall show later that they are too centralized. The legislative bodies encroach on the authority of the government every day, and their tendency, like that of the French Convention, is to take it entirely for themselves. In these circumstances the social power is constantly changing hands, because it is subordinate to the power of the people, which in its awareness of its own strength is all too ready to forget the maxims of wisdom and foresight. Here lies its danger. Its vigor, and not its weakness, will probably be the cause of its eventual destruction.

The system of local administration produces several different effects in America. The Americans seem to me to have gone beyond the limits of sound policy in isolating the administration of the government, for order, even in secondary matters, is of national importance. *r Because the State has no administrative officials of its own, stationed at various points across its territory, to whom it can give a common direction, it rarely tries to issue any general police regulations. The lack of these regulations is keenly felt, and Europeans frequently notice it. The appearance of disorder on the surface leads a European at first to imagine that society is in a state of anarchy, and he does not see his mistake until he has looked deeper into the subject. Certain undertakings matter to the whole State, but they cannot be carried out, because there is no national administration to direct them. Left to the efforts of the towns or counties, under the care of elected or temporary agents, they lead to no result, or at least to no lasting benefit.

r [ The authority that represents the State ought not, I think, to give up the right of inspecting the local administration, even when it does not intervene more actively. Suppose, for instance, that an agent of the government were stationed at some fixed place in the country to prosecute the misdemeanors of the town and county officers. Would not a more uniform order result, without in any way compromising the independence of the township? Nothing of the kind exists in America, however. There is nothing above the county courts, which have, as it were, only an incidental jurisdiction over the offenses they are meant to repress.]

The partisans of centralization in Europe are accustomed to maintain that the government directs the affairs of each locality better than the citizens could do it for themselves. This may be true when the central power is educated and the local districts are ignorant, when it is as quick as they are slow, and when it is used to acting while they are used to obeying. Indeed, it is plain that this double tendency must grow as centralization increases, and that the readiness of the one and the incapacity of the others must become more and more pronounced. But I deny that this is the case when the people is as well-informed, as alert to its interests, and as accustomed to reflect on them as the Americans are. I am convinced, on the contrary, that in this case the collective strength of the citizens will always serve the public welfare more effectively than the authority of the government. It is hard to say with certainty how to rouse a sleeping population and give it passions and knowledge it does not possess. I am well aware that it is a difficult task to persuade men to busy themselves with their own affairs, and it would often be easier to interest them in the fine points of court etiquette than in the repair of their common dwelling. But whenever a central administration claims to replace the people most concerned, I am inclined to suppose that it is either mistaken or trying to mislead. However enlightened and however skillful a central power may be, it cannot by itself take in all the details of the life of a great nation. Such vigilance is beyond human powers. And when it tries to build and set in motion so many complicated springs, it must accept a very imperfect result or wear itself out in futile efforts.

Centralization does succeed more easily in imposing a certain uniformity on the outward actions of men. This uniformity commands our respect for its own sake, whatever it is applied to, like those devotees who worship the statue and forget the deity it represents. Centralization gives an admirable regularity to the routine of business without difficulty. It attends to the details of public order with skill, represses the smallest disorder and the pettiest misdemeanors, and keeps society in a status quo that is safe alike from improvement and from decline. It perpetuates a drowsy precision in the conduct of affairs, which the heads of the administration welcome as a sign of perfect order and public tranquillity. *s In short, it is better at prevention than at action. Its force deserts it when society needs to be disturbed or hurried along in its course, and as soon as the cooperation of private citizens is necessary to carry out its measures, the secret of its weakness is exposed. Even while it asks for their help, it does so on the condition that they act exactly as much as the government chooses, and exactly in the manner it prescribes. They are to take charge of the details without aspiring to guide the system. They are to work in a dark and subordinate sphere, and to judge the acts they have helped to carry out only by their results. These are not the conditions on which the alliance of the human will can be won. Its bearing must be free and its actions responsible, or else (such is the nature of man) the citizen would rather remain a passive spectator than be a dependent actor in schemes he knows nothing about.

s [ China appears to me to offer the most perfect example of the kind of well-being that a completely centralized administration can provide for the nations under it. Travelers assure us that the Chinese have peace without happiness, industry without improvement, stability without strength, and public order without public morality. The condition of society is always tolerable, never excellent. I am convinced that when China is opened to European observation, it will be found to contain the most perfect model of a central administration that exists in the world.]

It cannot be denied that the United States not infrequently feels the lack of those uniform regulations that govern the conduct of every inhabitant of France. Gross cases of social indifference and neglect are to be found, and from time to time disgraceful blemishes appear in complete contrast with the civilization around them. Useful undertakings that cannot succeed without constant attention and rigorous exactness are very often abandoned in the end, for in America, as in other countries, the people is subject to sudden impulses and short bursts of effort. The European is accustomed to finding an official always at hand to interfere in everything he undertakes, and he has some difficulty getting used to the complex machinery of township administration. In general it may be said that the lesser details of police, which make life easy and comfortable, are neglected in America, but that the essential guarantees of man in society are as strong there as anywhere else. In America the power that conducts the government is far less regular, less enlightened, and less learned than in Europe, but a hundred times more authoritative. In no country in the world do the citizens make such efforts for the common good. I know of no people that has established schools as numerous and as effective, places of public worship better suited to the needs of the inhabitants, or roads kept in better repair. Uniformity and permanence of design, the minute arrangement of details, *t and the perfection of an ingenious administration must not be looked for in the United States.
