But it is easy to find there the signs of a power that, if somewhat barbarous, is at least robust, and of a life that is full of accidents, but also cheered by animation and effort.

t [ A writer of talent compared the finances of France with those of the United States, and in doing so proved that ingenuity cannot always take the place of a knowledge of facts. He very justly reproaches the Americans for the kind of confusion that exists in the accounts of township expenditure, and after giving the model of a departmental budget in France, he adds:—“We are indebted to centralization, that admirable invention of a great man, for the uniform order and method which prevail alike in all the municipal budgets, from the largest town to the humblest commune.” However much I may admire this result, I see the communes of France, with their excellent system of accounts, sunk in the grossest ignorance of their true interests and abandoned to so incurable an apathy that they seem to vegetate rather than to live. On the other hand, I observe the activity, the information, and the spirit of enterprise that keep society in perpetual labor in those American townships whose budgets are drawn up with little method and still less uniformity. The contrast strikes me, for in my view the purpose of a good government is to ensure the welfare of a people, and not to establish order and regularity in the midst of its misery and distress. I am therefore led to suppose that the prosperity of the American townships and the apparent confusion of their accounts, and the distress of the French communes and the perfection of their budget, may be due to the same cause. At any rate, I am suspicious of a benefit that comes with so many evils, and I do not mind an evil that is made up for by so many benefits.]

Suppose for a moment that the villages and counties of the United States would be governed more usefully by a distant authority they had never seen than by officials drawn from among themselves. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the country would be safer and the resources of society better used if the whole administration were centered in a single hand. Even so, the political advantages the Americans gain from their system would lead me to prefer it to the opposite plan. After all, it does me little good that a vigilant authority protects the tranquillity of my pleasures and constantly keeps every danger from my path, without any care or concern on my part, if this same authority is the absolute master of my liberty and my life. It does me little good if it so monopolizes all the energy of existence that when it languishes everything around it languishes, when it sleeps everything must sleep, and when it dies the state itself must perish.

In certain countries of Europe the natives regard themselves as a kind of settlers, indifferent to the fate of the place where they live. The greatest changes are carried out without their participation and, unless chance happens to inform them, without their knowledge. What is more, the citizen is unconcerned about the condition of his village, the policing of his street, or the repair of the church or the parsonage. He looks on all these things as having nothing to do with himself, and as the property of a powerful stranger whom he calls the government. He has only a life interest in these possessions, and he has no idea of ownership or of improvement. This lack of interest in his own affairs goes so far that if his own safety or that of his children is in danger, he will not try to avert the peril. Instead he will fold his arms and wait for the nation to come to his assistance. This same man, who has so completely given up his own free will, has no natural inclination to obedience. He cowers, it is true, before the pettiest official, but he defies the law with the spirit of a conquered enemy as soon as its superior force is removed. He swings constantly between servitude and license. When a nation has reached this state, it must either change its customs and its laws or perish. The source of public virtue is dry, and though the nation may still contain subjects, the race of citizens is extinct. Such communities are a natural prey to foreign conquest. If they do not disappear from the scene, it is because they are surrounded by other nations similar or inferior to themselves. It is because the instinctive feeling for their country’s claims still lives in their hearts, and because an involuntary pride in its name, or a vague memory of its past glory, is enough to give them the impulse of self-preservation.

Nor can the prodigious efforts that tribes have made in defense of a country that was not their own be cited in favor of such a system. In these cases it will be found that their main motive was religion. The permanence, the glory, or the prosperity of the nation had become part of their faith, and in defending the country they lived in, they defended that Holy City of which they were all citizens. The Turkish tribes never took an active part in the conduct of public affairs, yet they accomplished stupendous enterprises as long as the victories of the Sultan were the triumphs of the Mohammedan faith. In the present age they are in rapid decay, because their religion is departing and only despotism remains. Montesquieu attributed to absolute power an authority peculiar to itself, and in doing so, I think, he gave it an honor it did not deserve, for despotism, taken by itself, can produce no lasting results. On close inspection we shall find that religion, and not fear, has always been the cause of the long-lived prosperity of an absolute government. Whatever efforts may be made, no true power can be founded among men that does not rest on the free union of their inclinations. Patriotism and religion are the only two motives in the world that can permanently direct a whole body politic toward one end.

Laws cannot rekindle the ardor of an extinguished faith, but they can make men take an interest in the fate of their country. Through this influence the vague impulse of patriotism, which never abandons the human heart, may be directed and revived. If it is connected with the thoughts, the passions, and the daily habits of life, it may be consolidated into a lasting and rational feeling.
Do not say that the time for the experiment has already passed. Nations do not grow old the way men do, and each new generation is a fresh people, waiting for the legislator’s care.

It is not the administrative effects but the political effects of the local system that I admire most in America. In the United States the interests of the country are kept in view everywhere. They are an object of concern to the people of the whole Union, and every citizen is as warmly attached to them as if they were his own. He takes pride in the glory of his nation. He boasts of its successes, to which he believes he has contributed, and he rejoices in the general prosperity from which he profits. The feeling he has toward the State is like the one that binds him to his family, and it is through a kind of egotism that he takes an interest in the welfare of his country.

The European generally submits to a public official because the official represents a superior force. To an American, the official represents a right. In America it may be said that no one obeys man, but only justice and the law. If the opinion a citizen holds of himself is exaggerated, it is at least healthy. He confidently trusts in his own powers, which appear to him to be all-sufficient. When a private individual plans an undertaking, however directly it may concern the welfare of society, he never thinks of asking for the cooperation of the government. He publishes his plan, offers to carry it out himself, seeks the help of other individuals, and struggles manfully against all obstacles. No doubt he is often less successful than the State would have been in his place, but in the end the sum of these private undertakings far exceeds anything the government could have done.

Because the administrative authority is within the reach of the citizens, whom it in some degree represents, it arouses neither their jealousy nor their hatred. Because its resources are limited, everyone feels that he must not rely on its assistance alone. Thus, when the administration sees fit to intervene, it is not left to itself as it is in Europe. The duties of private citizens are not supposed to have lapsed because the State helps in carrying them out. On the contrary, everyone is ready to guide and support it. This combination of individual efforts with those of the public authorities often accomplishes what the most energetic central administration would be unable to do. It would be easy to cite several facts in proof of what I say, but I prefer to give only one, with which I am better acquainted. *u In America the means that the authorities have for discovering crimes and arresting criminals are few. There is no State police, and passports are unknown. The criminal police of the United States cannot be compared to that of France. The magistrates and public prosecutors are not numerous, and the examinations of prisoners are quick and oral. Nevertheless, in no country does crime more rarely escape punishment. The reason is that everyone considers himself concerned in providing evidence of the act committed and in stopping the offender. During my stay in the United States I saw committees form spontaneously to pursue and prosecute a man who had committed a great crime in a certain county. In Europe a criminal is an unhappy being struggling for his life against the ministers of justice, while the population merely watches the conflict. In America he is looked on as an enemy of the human race, and the whole of mankind is against him.
u [ See Appendix, I.]

I believe that provincial institutions benefit every nation, but nowhere do they seem to me more necessary than among a democratic people. In an aristocracy, order can always be kept even amid liberty, and since the rulers have a great deal to lose, order is their first concern. In the same way, an aristocracy shields the people from the excesses of despotism, because it always has an organized power ready to resist a despot. A democracy without provincial institutions has no protection against either evil. How can a populace that has never been used to freedom in small matters learn to use it with moderation in great affairs? What resistance can be offered to tyranny in a country where every private individual is powerless and no common tie unites the citizens? Those who dread the license of the mob, and those who fear the rule of absolute power, ought equally to want provincial liberties to grow steadily.

On the other hand, I am convinced that democratic nations are the most exposed to falling under the yoke of a central administration, for several reasons, among them the following. The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the government in the hands of the only power that directly represents the people, because beyond the people nothing can be seen but a mass of equal individuals merged together. But when that same power already holds all the attributes of government, it can hardly refrain from reaching into the details of administration, and an opportunity to do so is sure to present itself in the end, as happened in France. In the French Revolution there were two impulses in opposite directions, which must never be confused. One favored liberty, the other despotism. Under the ancient monarchy the King was the sole author of the laws, and beneath the sovereign’s power certain half-destroyed vestiges of provincial institutions could still be made out. These provincial institutions were incoherent, loosely constructed, and often absurd. In the hands of the aristocracy they had sometimes been turned into instruments of oppression. The Revolution declared itself the enemy of royalty and of provincial institutions at the same time. It lumped together everything that had come before it, despotic power and the checks on its abuses alike, in indiscriminate hatred, and its tendency was both to overthrow and to centralize. This double character of the French Revolution is a fact that the friends of absolute power have skillfully handled. Can they be accused of working for despotism when they defend that central administration, which was one of the great innovations of the Revolution? *v In this way popularity may be won along with hostility to the rights of the people, and the secret slave of tyranny may be the professed admirer of freedom.
v [ See Appendix K.]

I have visited the two nations where the system of provincial liberty is most fully established, and I listened to what different parties there had to say. In America I met men who secretly hoped to destroy the democratic institutions of the Union. In England I found others who openly attacked the aristocracy. Yet I know of no one in either country who does not regard provincial independence as a great benefit. In both countries I heard a thousand different causes named for the evils of the State, but the local system was never among them. I heard citizens credit the power and prosperity of their country to a multitude of reasons, but all of them put the advantages of local institutions first. Am I to suppose that men who are so divided by nature in religious opinion and political theory are all mistaken when they agree on one point, and one they experience every day? The only nations that deny the usefulness of provincial liberties are those that have the fewest of them. In other words, only those who do not know the institution condemn it.
